title: Four-Class Alzheimer MRI Classification
cardEyebrow: Four-class MRI classification and ensemble learning
summary: A complete TensorFlow MRI experiment that turns 6,400 ADNI brain MRI images into a four-class training pipeline, compares independently saved CNNs, and raises held-out accuracy from 78% to 85% through probability-level ensembling.
landingDeck: The study connects data inspection, performant TensorFlow ingestion, training-only augmentation, two CNN scales, reusable inference, image-level error review, checkpoint reuse, and two- and three-model probability ensembles inside one inspectable Colab workflow.
landingHighlights: Processes 6,400 MRI files across NonDemented, VeryMildDemented, MildDemented, and ModerateDemented classes with a recorded 5,120/640/640-image split.
Compares a 2.11-million-parameter six-block CNN with a saved 491,524-parameter variant, then composes independently trained checkpoints into common evaluable graphs.
Reports a seven-percentage-point held-out improvement in the companion experiment, from a 78% single-model baseline to an 85% ensemble result.
problem: Four-class dementia-stage classification requires a model to separate adjacent categories whose MRI slices can appear structurally similar. The research question extends beyond fitting one CNN: can independently trained variants contribute complementary judgments when their full class-probability vectors are combined?
approach: The Colab workflow discovers 6,400 folder-labeled ADNI brain MRI scans, inspects their visual characteristics, builds cached and prefetched TensorFlow partitions, applies training-only augmentation, trains and reloads CNN variants, renders class-and-confidence review grids, and evaluates equal-average two- and three-model ensembles on the held-out stream. Network depth, width, normalization, and dropout were tuned across variants: the main network uses six convolutional blocks growing from 64 to 256 filters with 30% dropout and a 512-unit classifier, and the lighter variant uses 32 to 128 filters with a 128-unit classifier.
output: A 100-cell experimental notebook with retained dataset and model evidence, a reproducible 256×256 four-class pipeline, deep and compact CNN variants, reusable single-image and grid inference, probability-level checkpoint fusion, and a documented seven-point companion-experiment gain.

methodology.evaluation: Retained outputs verify 6,400 files, four labels, 100 batches, an 80/10/10 partition, 256×256×3 tensors, a 2,114,756-parameter main CNN, and a 491,524-parameter saved CNN. The companion experiment reports 78% baseline and 85% ensemble accuracy; the public notebook separately records a 13% improvement statement alongside its three-model evaluation code.
methodology.boundary: The work is a retrospective image-classification study. A later clinical validation program would add subject-level partition manifests, repeated-seed and class-wise statistics, scanner-diverse external data, calibration, and clinical review.

role: I designed and built the complete notebook experiment: ADNI data discovery and inspection, TensorFlow preprocessing and augmentation, CNN architecture design and hyperparameter tuning (depth, width, normalization, dropout), training, checkpoint loading, reusable inference, sample-level error review, two- and three-model probability ensembles, weighted-fusion exploration, evaluation calls, visualizations, and run documentation.

pageSections.title: The study inspects the images before asking a network to classify them
pageSections.markdown:
The loader reports exactly 6,400 files belonging to four classes and retains their alphabetical class-index order. A saved batch confirms tensors shaped **64 × 256 × 256 × 3** with integer labels, while the 12-image montage lets the researcher inspect representative scans and category labels before training begins.

The notebook also measures the black-background fraction in sampled scans using two OpenCV and NumPy approaches. Recorded examples contain approximately 48.0% and 46.47% black pixels. These samples are exploratory checks, and they surface a central imaging consideration: a large share of each slice may carry no anatomy while still influencing resizing, convolution, and augmentation.

The pipeline converts the 100 batches into 80 training, ten validation, and ten test batches. Each stream is cached, shuffled, and prefetched with `tf.data.AUTOTUNE`. Training images receive horizontal and vertical flips, 0.2 rotation, 0.2 width and height variation, and 0.1 zoom. Validation and test scans keep their unaugmented evaluation path. The resulting workflow automates input standardization and varied training views while keeping the held-out streams comparable.

pageSections.title: Model diversity is made concrete through scale, checkpoints, and shared evaluation

items.label: Primary CNN
items.title: 2,114,756 trainable parameters
items.body: Six convolutional blocks progress through 64, 64, 128, 256, 256, and 256 filters, each followed by 2×2 max pooling, then 30% dropout and a 512-unit dense representation.

items.label: Compact checkpoint
items.title: 491,524 trainable parameters
items.body: A separately saved six-block network uses 32, 64, 64, 128, 128, and 128 filters with a 128-unit dense layer, providing a materially different scale for comparison and fusion.

items.label: Common task
items.title: One four-class input and evaluation contract
items.body: Each model receives the same 256×256×3 input shape, produces a four-value softmax vector, and can be evaluated through the same sparse-cross-entropy and accuracy workflow.

items.label: Reusable inference
items.title: Class and confidence remain inspectable
items.body: A shared helper converts raw predictions into the class name and maximum softmax confidence used by both individual models and ensembles.

pageSections.title: The notebook combines model judgments before information is discarded
pageSections.markdown:
The two-model graph sends one MRI through the primary network and a saved variant, then averages their complete four-class softmax vectors. The three-model graph repeats the operation across three independently saved checkpoints. Final class selection happens only after fusion.

This late-fusion design retains each model's relative support for every category. Agreement strengthens a decision; disagreement lets one network's uncertain or idiosyncratic output be moderated by the others. It uses more information than voting over final labels and avoids the additional training protocol required by a learned meta-classifier.

The implementation also improves the research workflow. Saved checkpoints become composable Keras graph components that share an input, evaluation stream, loss, accuracy metric, and inference helper. Single-model, two-model, and three-model behavior can therefore be compared inside the same notebook instead of through disconnected manual runs. A custom weighted layer begins the next experiment by assigning proposed weights of 0.3, 0.6, and 0.1.

pageSections.title: Probability ensembling improved held-out accuracy from 78% to 85%
pageSections.markdown: The companion experiment records a 78% single-model baseline and an 85% ensemble result: a seven-percentage-point gain, approximately 9% relative to the baseline. The public notebook independently contains the matching four-class pipeline, saved-model loading, equal-average two- and three-model graphs, compilation, test evaluation calls, and a separate markdown statement describing a 13% improvement for its three-model comparison. These are two recorded comparisons, so the portfolio assigns each result to its own experiment record.

pageSections.title: The experiment grows in controlled steps from data inspection to model consensus

items.label: Observe
items.title: Begin with the data distribution and image content
items.body: Count files, verify class order and batch shape, view real samples, and inspect background occupancy before selecting transformations.

items.label: Control
items.title: Keep training variation separate from evaluation
items.body: Apply augmentation to the training stream and retain dedicated validation and test partitions for comparison.

items.label: Establish
items.title: Train and inspect a convolutional baseline
items.body: Record architecture, parameter count, learning curves, evaluation calls, and sample predictions in the same executable document.

items.label: Diversify
items.title: Reload models with meaningfully different capacities
items.body: Use separately trained saved variants as independent probability estimators with distinct capacities and decision boundaries.

items.label: Fuse
items.title: Compare equal and weighted probability combinations
items.body: Evaluate two-model and three-model averages, then prototype a weighted layer for the next controlled comparison.

items.label: Interpret
items.title: Return aggregate results to individual images
items.body: Review actual label, predicted label, and confidence together to identify the scans behind correct and incorrect decisions.

pageSections.title: I designed and built the full classification and ensemble experiment
pageSections.markdown: I implemented the notebook's data discovery, labeled image inspection, black-background exploration, TensorFlow partitioning and performance pipeline, resizing and rescaling, training-only augmentation, six-block CNN, architecture visualization, checkpoint persistence and loading, reusable class-and-confidence inference, image-level error-review grids, two- and three-model probability ensembles, weighted-fusion exploration, test evaluation calls, and documentation for reproducing the workflow.

pageSections.title: A rigorous retrospective MRI classification study and ensemble result
pageSections.markdown:
The repository implements the complete image-level experiment and retains evidence for its data scale, partitions, tensor shape, model structures, and inference workflow. The companion experiment supplies the 78% to 85% held-out comparison.

A clinical validation program would extend this work with subject-level separation, repeated runs, confusion matrices and class-wise statistics, scanner-diverse external data, calibration, and clinical review.
